Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Location: Going to or near the place where the event happened, Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
The night operation in the Helmand Valley had been routine until the road collapsed. Thomas remembered the sudden drop, the jarring impact of his vehicle against the dry riverbed, and the sharp, overlapping cracks of small arms fire echoing off the limestone cliffs. He had dragged two men out of the wreckage, feeling the weight of their bodies slip through his grip as the desert heat baked the dust into his lungs. When the dust finally settled, only he and the medic had walked away. Thomas told himself they had done everything they could, but the silence that followed felt heavier than the sand. Over the decades, that specific stretch of cracked earth and limestone canyon became a place he could not stand to visit, and any topography that mirrored it—a dry wash, a steep embankment, a narrow road cutting through canyon walls—prompted him to take a detour without explaining why. At first, the memories came as clear, unbidden flashes. But as the years passed, Thomas found his mind refusing to give him the narrative he wanted or needed. He knew exactly what had happened, yet when he tried to pull the details together, his tongue grew heavy and the images remained trapped behind a wall of static. If he pushed himself to remember, the terror returned with the same physical force—the tight chest, the shallow breaths, the certainty that he was out of time. Alongside that panic came a sharp, familiar guilt. He would sit in his recliner, staring at the wall, and a quiet, persistent weight would settle in his stomach. He kept thinking of the names he could no longer visit, and the thought that he was the one still here, breathing in a quiet suburban kitchen, felt like a betrayal. What frightened him most was not the violence itself, but the way his own mind refused to let him make sense of it, leaving only the raw, wordless terror and the heavy sense that he owed his survival to those who did not get to keep theirs. Over time, Thomas built a careful routine around what he could no longer tolerate. He stopped going to the hardware store that sold military surplus because the olive drab jackets hanging in the window mirrored the uniforms he had worn. He traded his old work boots for soft-soled sneakers, convinced that the heavy tread and scuffed leather would drag him back to that riverbed. He learned to deflect conversations that grew quiet or turned toward the past, changing the subject or walking to the garage to tune the radio until the noise filled the space. The world outside had slowly shifted in his perception. What had once felt like a predictable place had become a landscape of constant, quiet danger, and he found himself scanning exits and checking the structural integrity of overpasses without acknowledging why. He also noticed a strange distance between himself and the man he used to be. His hands, once calloused and sure, now felt like foreign tools, and he caught himself looking in the mirror and not recognizing the eyes staring back. He did not know how to bridge the gap between the soldier who had walked away and the husband sitting across from his partner at the dinner table. His job at the distribution warehouse became a daily test of these habits. The safety vest they issued was a bright, reflective orange, but the cut and the heavy nylon straps ran exactly like his old tactical gear. On his third week back from a brief leave, Thomas had stood frozen in aisle four, the vest suddenly feeling like it was choking him. He had quietly slipped it off, rolled it into a bundle, and asked his supervisor for a plain T-shirt under the vest, claiming it was too warm. He never explained that the fabric felt like a reminder of the weight on his shoulders, and the incident had cost him a promotion he had been preparing for months to earn. They stopped sharing long evenings. When a car backfired outside, Thomas would flinch and suddenly stop speaking, his jaw tight, eyes fixed on the far wall as if searching for a way out of a conversation he could no longer navigate. At sixty, Thomas finally walked into the clinic because the silence in his own house had grown too loud to bear. Clara had left a brochure on the counter after he accidentally packed two sets of boots for a weekend trip, one pair heavy and laced, the other soft and new, and he had spent the entire morning standing in the driveway staring at them. He was terrified that he was losing the ability to stay present with the people he loved, and he was afraid that the world outside his door would keep getting narrower until there was nowhere left to stand. He hoped, however faintly, to find a way to stop bracing for the ground to give way beneath him, and to finally learn how to speak about the night without his voice catching in his throat.
